entry: Social gathering of invited guests, typically for conversation, recreation, or a celebration. A party often features food and beverages, along with conversation, music, dancing, or other entertainment. Some parties honor a specific person, day, or event, such as a [[Birthday|birthday]] party or a [[Super Bowl]] party; these are often called celebrations. A party is not necessarily private. Public parties are held in parks, restaurants, pubs, beer gardens, nightclubs, or [[Bar (establishment)|bars]], and hosts or venues may charge admission. Large parties in public streets may mark events such as [[Mardi Gras]] or the signing of a peace treaty ending a long war. Western birthday parties include common rituals: guests may bring gifts, a [[Cake|cake]] is served with lit candles to be blown out after a wish, and the guests sing a birthday song. Historically, English speakers also called some gatherings "drums" or "assemblies."

Principal goddess of [[Hinduism]], consort of [[Shiva]]. Also known as Uma and Gauri, she is revered as the goddess of power, energy, nourishment, love, beauty, devotion, and motherhood. She first appears as a goddess in the epic period (400 BCE–400 CE). With [[Lakshmi]] and Sarasvati, she forms the *Tridevi*, a trinity of goddesses. Puranic texts describe her as the reincarnation of Sati, Shiva's first wife, and her birth to the mountain lord Himavan is understood as a cosmic event that drew Shiva into married life. She is regarded as Shiva's *shakti*, the creative force that sustains the cosmos, and as the mother of [[Ganesha]] and [[Kartikeya]]. Often equated with [[Durga]], she is regarded in [[Shaktism]] as a benevolent aspect of Mahadevi. Her statues appear in Hindu temples throughout [[South Asia]] and Southeast Asia.

Infinite triangular array of binomial coefficients, used in [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]], [[Probability theory|probability theory]], and algebra. Each entry is the sum of the two numbers above it, starting from a single 1 at the apex. The nth row gives the coefficients in the expansion of (a + b)ⁿ, linking the array to the [[Binomial theorem|binomial theorem]]. In much of the Western world it is named after French mathematician [[Blaise Pascal]], although mathematicians in India, Persia, China, Germany, and Italy studied it centuries earlier. Persian mathematician [[Omar Khayyam]] applied its coefficients to extracting nth roots.

Philosophical argument for believing in [[God]], advanced by [[Blaise Pascal]]. A rational person should wager on God's existence. If God does not exist, the believer loses only certain pleasures. If God exists, the believer gains an eternity in [[Heaven]] and avoids an eternity in [[Hell]]. Reason cannot settle the question, so a wager is unavoidable. The argument appears in the posthumous *Pensées* ("Thoughts") and is regarded as the first formal application of decision theory. Critics question whether God's existence can be proven, note conflicting religious claims to revelation, and contend that belief motivated by gain is not genuine.

Unit of [[Pressure|pressure]] in the [[International System of Units]] (SI). The pascal (Pa) is defined as the pressure exerted by a force of one newton on an area of one square meter, or one newton per square meter (N/m²). In SI base units it equals one kilogram per meter per second squared (kg/(m·s²)). The unit is named after [[Blaise Pascal]], noted for his work on hydrodynamics, hydrostatics, and experiments with a barometer, and it was adopted by the 14th General Conference on Weights and Measures in 1971. Because the pascal is small, larger multiples are common: the kilopascal (kPa) and the hectopascal (hPa), which equals one millibar. The [[Standard atmosphere (unit)|standard atmosphere]] is defined as 101,325 Pa, and meteorologists report sea-level pressure in hectopascals, typically about 1,013 hPa. Engineers prefer the megapascal (MPa) for the [[Stress (mechanics)|stress]], tensile strength, and stiffness of materials.

Eastern Iranian language of the Indo-European family, spoken natively in northwestern [[Pakistan]] and southern and eastern [[Afghanistan]]. Pashto is one of Afghanistan's two official languages, alongside Dari, and the second-largest language in Pakistan, spoken mainly in [[Khyber Pakhtunkhwa]]. It is the native language of most [[Pashtuns]], and estimates of its speakers range from 35 million to 55 million. It is written in a modified [[Arabic script]] with additional letters. Persian remained more widely used in government, but a 1936 royal decree formally granted Pashto official status. Speakers also live in India, Iran, [[Tajikistan]], the [[United Arab Emirates]], and [[Saudi Arabia]], where Pashtun diaspora communities are large. Pashto has Northern and Southern dialects.

Iranian ethnic group of southern and eastern [[Afghanistan]] and northwestern [[Pakistan]]. Pashtuns speak [[Pashto]] and are called Pathans in India. They form the world's largest tribal society, with 60–70 million people and between 350–400 tribes. Estimates are disputed because Afghanistan has had no official census since 1979. They are the largest ethnic group in Afghanistan, at around 42–47% of its population, and the second-largest in Pakistan, at around 18.24%. The world's largest urban Pashtun community is in [[Karachi]]. Pashtunwali, an unwritten code emphasizing hospitality and honor, is central to Pashtun identity.

Extinct migratory pigeon of eastern and central [[North America]], *Ectopistes migratorius*. Its name comes from the French *passager*, "passing by," reflecting its migrations. The birds moved in enormous flocks through deciduous forests and bred mainly around the [[Great Lakes]]. Once the most abundant bird in North America, it numbered around 3 billion, possibly up to 5 billion. It could fly at 100 km/h (62 mph). Native Americans hunted it, but [[Hunting|hunting]] intensified after European arrival, and the meat was sold as cheap food on a massive scale. [[Deforestation|Deforestation]] destroyed its habitat, and the population fell slowly from about 1800 to 1870, then rapidly until 1890. A plaque in Indiana states that the last confirmed wild bird was shot in Laurel in 1902. Martha, thought to be the last of the species, died at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914. Its loss is a notable example of [[Extinction|anthropogenic extinction]].

[[Merchant ship]] whose primary function is carrying passengers at sea. Passenger ships are part of the merchant marine, but they have also been used as troopships and are often commissioned as naval ships. The traditional form is the [[Ocean liner|ocean liner]], which ran scheduled voyages between inhabited parts of the world and usually carried mail and freight as well. Ferries carry passengers and vehicles on short or overnight trips, while [[Cruise ship|cruise ships]] carry passengers on round trips, where the voyage and its amenities are the main attraction. Ocean liners emphasized speed and traditional luxury and were often built to cross the [[Atlantic Ocean]] between Europe and the [[United States]]. Cruise ships value amenities such as pools and casinos over speed, and since the 1980s they have grown to carry hundreds to thousands of people, with activity centered in the [[Caribbean Sea]].

[[Bird]] of the order Passeriformes, also called a perching bird. Passerines have an anisodactyl foot, with three toes forward and one back, which helps them perch. The largest order of birds includes more than 140 families and some 6,500 species, about 60% of all birds. It has three suborders: the New Zealand wrens, the suboscines of the [[Americas]], and the [[Songbird|songbirds]]. The name derives from *passer*, Latin for sparrow, after the [[House sparrow]], *Passer domesticus*. Passerines originated in the Southern Hemisphere around 60 million years ago. Most are insectivorous or omnivorous. The heaviest are the thick-billed raven and the larger [[Common raven|common raven]], each exceeding 1.5 kg (3.3 lb). Chicks are altricial, hatching blind and featherless, so they need extensive parental care.

Major Jewish holiday commemorating the Exodus of the [[Israelites]] from slavery in Egypt. Also called *Pesach*, it is one of the Three Pilgrimage Festivals. According to the Book of Exodus in the [[Torah]], God commanded Moses to tell the Israelites to mark their doorframes with the blood of a lamb, so that the tenth plague, which would kill the firstborn in Egypt, would pass over their homes. After that plague, the [[Pharaoh]] let them leave. The story is retold at the Seder using the Haggadah. Jews are forbidden from possessing or eating leavened foods (*chametz*) during the holiday. It begins on the 15th day of the Hebrew month of Nisan, at sundown the evening before, and lasts seven days in Israel and eight in the Diaspora. Scholars widely believe Passover originated separately from the biblical Exodus and was later transformed.

Government-issued travel document certifying the holder's identity and nationality. A passport allows its bearer to enter and temporarily reside in a foreign country, obtain consular assistance, and receive local aid. Passports are a key tool for border security and for regulating [[Immigration|migration]], and they may also serve as identity documents at home. The booklet bears the issuing government's name and emblem and contains the holder's name, photograph, biographical details, and signature. It does not create rights in the country visited but certifies identity and the right to travel. [[Citizenship|Citizenship]] is a common prerequisite, although some nationals without full citizenship rights may receive passports. The modern passport was universally adopted and standardized in 1920, and since 1998 many countries have issued biometric passports with an embedded microchip. Over 150 jurisdictions issued such e-passports as of July 2024.

Secret data, typically a string of characters, used to confirm a user's identity. Passwords were expected to be memorized, but the many services a person uses make unique memorized passwords impractical. A passphrase is a longer memorized secret made of words, and a numeric-only password is called a personal identification number (PIN). Computer passwords appeared in the early 1960s at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], where they protected files on shared mainframes. Passwords remain vulnerable to guessing and [[Phishing|phishing]], so [[Multi-factor authentication|multi-factor authentication]] is often added.

Set of all events that occurred before a given point in time. The past is defined in contrast with the present and the [[Future|future]]. It is accessed through [[Memory|memory]] and recollection, and humans have recorded it since the advent of written language. In [[Grammar|grammar]], the past tense describes actions already completed, as in "she walked," and the past perfect describes an action completed before another past moment. The English word derives from a variant of *passed*, the past participle of the [[Middle English]] verb *passen*. In philosophy, presentism holds that only the present is real, while eternalism holds that past, present, and future coexist equally. Historians reconstruct the past from evidence, often revising accounts as new sources emerge.

Food of unleavened dough, usually made from wheat flour mixed with water or eggs, shaped and cooked by boiling or baking. Pasta was originally made only with durum wheat, but the term now includes gluten-free versions made from rice flour or from [[Legume|legumes]] such as beans or [[Lentil|lentils]]. It is a staple of [[Italian cuisine]]. Dried pasta is usually made by [[Extrusion|extrusion]], while fresh pasta is traditionally made by hand. Some 310 specific forms are known by over 1,300 documented names. Pasta is served in three classic ways: with a sauce, in broth as soup, or baked in a dish. Many historians believe pasta in a recognizable form reached Italy through [[Sicily]] in the [[Middle Ages]], via Mediterranean [[Trade|trade]] networks, though claims of Etruscan pasta lack sufficient evidence.

Process of preserving foods, such as [[Milk|milk]] and fruit juices, with mild heat. Packaged foods are heated to less than 100 °C (212 °F) to destroy or deactivate [[Microorganism|microorganisms]] and enzymes that cause spoilage or disease, including most vegetative bacteria, though most bacterial spores survive. The process is named after French microbiologist [[Louis Pasteur]], whose research in the 1860s showed that heat could deactivate unwanted microorganisms in wine. It is widely used in the [[Dairy|dairy]] industry. Because the heat is mild, the nutritional quality and taste of treated foods change only slightly. Milk is commonly heated to 72°C for 15 seconds, or to 63°C for 30 minutes. Non-thermal methods such as high-pressure processing and pulsed electric field treatment are also used.

Unleavened dough, often enriched with fat or eggs, and the baked goods made from it. Common pastry dishes include *börek*, [[Pie|pies]], tarts, and turnovers. Solid fat keeps gluten from forming elastic strands in the [[Flour|flour]], which gives pastry its short, flaky, or crumbly texture. Shortcrust pastry follows a classic 3:2:1 ratio of flour, fat, and water. Puff pastry is a laminated dough folded into hundreds of thin layers and used for elegant sweets or savory dishes such as [[Beef|beef]] Wellington. Choux pastry is cooked on the stovetop before baking, producing light shapes such as éclairs. Filo consists of ultra-thin sheets brushed with fat and is used in [[Baklava]]. In North America the term usually means sweet baked goods.

Geographical region at the southern tip of [[South America]], governed by Argentina and Chile. It includes the southern [[Andes]], with lakes, fjords, temperate rainforests, and glaciers in the west, and deserts, tablelands, and [[Steppe|steppes]] to the east. Many waterways connect the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, including the [[Strait of Magellan]], the Beagle Channel, and the [[Drake Passage]]. Before Spanish arrival, most groups were hunter-gatherers, and the reintroduced horse later supported nomadic life in the northeast. After independence, Chile and Argentina colonized the region in the 19th and early 20th centuries, which disrupted indigenous societies. Today Argentine Patagonia relies on sheep farming and oil and [[Natural gas|natural gas]], while Chilean Patagonia depends on fishing, salmon aquaculture, and tourism. The name comes from *patagón*, a term [[Ferdinand Magellan|Magellan]] used in 1520 for indigenous people he thought were giants.

Ancient Indian author or authors, traditionally credited with the *Yoga Sutras*. Scholars now generally accept that several authors shared the name, though tradition often attributes their works to one person. The *Yoga Sutras* is the classical text of [[Yoga|yoga]] theory and practice, and it outlines the eightfold path toward liberation. Estimates date its author or authors between the 2nd century BCE and the 5th century CE. A different Patanjali wrote the *Mahābhāṣya*, a commentary on Sanskrit grammar based on the work of [[Pāṇini]], dated to the 2nd century BCE. Another Patanjali is credited with a medical text, the *Patanjalatantra*. Tradition regards him as an avatar of Adi Sesha.

Form of [[Intellectual property|intellectual property]] giving its owner the legal right to exclude others from making, using, or selling an invention for a limited period. In exchange, the owner publishes an enabling disclosure of the invention, so society receives the invention rather than secrecy. In most countries patent rights fall under private law, so the holder must sue infringers to enforce them. Under the [[World Trade Organization]]'s TRIPS Agreement, patents should be available for new inventions that involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application, for a minimum term of twenty years. The word derives from Latin *patere*, "to lay open." The first statutory patent system is generally regarded as the [[Republic of Venice|Venetian]] Patent Statute of 1474. In the [[United States]], the first patent statute dates from 1790. Critics argue that overbroad grants can impede cumulative progress.

Organism or agent that can produce disease, also called an infectious agent or germ. The term came into use in the 1880s. Pathogens typically include [[Virus|viruses]], [[Bacteria|bacteria]], [[Protozoa|protozoa]], [[Fungus|fungi]], prions, and viroids. Small animals such as helminths and insects are usually called parasites instead. Pathogenicity combines infectivity, the ability to infect hosts, and virulence, the severity of disease. Infection can spread through direct contact, contaminated surfaces, airborne droplets, or vectors such as [[Mosquito|mosquitoes]] and [[Tick|ticks]]. [[Tuberculosis]], primarily caused by *Mycobacterium tuberculosis*, killed 1.6 million people in 2021. Some pathogens cause disease only in hosts with immunodeficiency, and some diseases, such as sickle cell disease and [[Lupus|lupus]], are not caused by pathogens.

Study of disease, especially its diagnosis through examination of [[Tissue (biology)|tissues]] and cells. In modern medicine the term usually refers to general pathology, a field of specialties that analyze samples for diagnosis and research. A physician who practices it is called a pathologist. General pathology has two major specialties, anatomical pathology and clinical pathology, which are further divided by sample type, organ, or purpose, as with forensic pathology. The field examines the cause of disease, its development (pathogenesis), structural changes in cells, and clinical manifestations. Study of disease dates to antiquity, and [[Hippocrates]] developed methods of diagnosis and prognosis in ancient Greece. In the 17th century, examination of tissue led [[Robert Hooke]] to coin the word "[[Cell (biology)|cell]]." Modern pathology emerged as a distinct field in the 19th century.

Capital and largest city of the [[India|Indian]] state of [[Bihar]]. Patna lies mainly on the southern bank of the [[Ganges]] and straddles the Son, Gandak, and Punpun rivers. Founded in 490 BCE by the king of [[Magadha]], it was known as Pataliputra and served as the capital of the Magadha Empire through several dynasties, including the Mauryan and [[Gupta Empire|Gupta]]. Pataliputra was a center of learning, home to astronomers and scholars including [[Aryabhata]] and [[Chanakya]]. After the fall of the Gupta Empire it declined, and the British revived it in the 17th century as a trading center. Following the partition of Bengal Presidency in 1912, it became the capital of Bihar and Orissa Province. Patna is sacred to Sikhs, as [[Guru Gobind Singh]] was born there. The city covers 250 sq km and is the seat of the Patna High Court.

Cleric of the [[Russian Orthodox Church]] and seventh Patriarch of [[Moscow]] and all Rus'. Nikon was the son of a peasant farmer and became a monk before rising to the patriarchate. He was close to [[Alexis of Russia|Tsar Alexis]], who appointed him to the Novospassky monastery in Moscow, associated with the [[House of Romanov|Romanov]] dynasty. He was elected patriarch in 1652 and served until 1666. As patriarch he introduced liturgical reforms, including standardized service books and the three-finger sign of the cross, that were unpopular with conservatives. The reforms led to a lasting schism, the Raskol, and to resistance from the [[Old Believers]]. For many years he was a dominant political figure, sometimes equaling or overshadowing the tsar. In December 1667 a church synod deprived him of his priestly functions and reduced him to the rank of simple monk.

Congolese independence leader and first prime minister of the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo|Congo]]. Lumumba led the Congolese National Movement (MNC) from 1958 and served as prime minister from June to September 1960, after his party won the May 1960 election. An African nationalist and pan-Africanist, he played a major role in turning the [[Belgium|Belgian]] Congo into an independent republic. Shortly after independence, army mutinies and the secession of Katanga and South Kasai led him to send the army against the breakaway regions. President Joseph Kasa-Vubu dismissed him, and a coup led by [[Mobutu Sese Seko|Mobutu]] followed. Captured under Mobutu's authority, Lumumba was transferred to Katanga, where separatist authorities tortured and executed him. In 2002 Belgium formally apologized for its role in his death. He is widely seen as a martyr of anticolonial liberation.
